prompt: Adjacency list vs adjacency matrix: state the space cost of each and the one question that decides which to use.
reveal: Two ways to store a graph's edges. An **adjacency list** keeps, per vertex, a list of its neighbors — total size **O(V+E)** (V vertices plus E edges). An **adjacency matrix** is a V×V grid where cell (i,j) marks whether the edge i→j exists — size **O(V²)** no matter how few edges there actually are. The one deciding question is **density**: reach for the matrix only when the graph is **dense** (edge count E approaches V², the maximum possible) or you need **O(1)** "does this edge exist?" lookups; otherwise use lists. **Tell:** most graphs are sparse, so the interview default is the adjacency list.

practice.label: LeetCode 1971. Find if Path Exists in Graph

prompt: When does BFS give you a shortest path and when does it fail? What replaces it when it fails?
reveal: BFS (breadth-first search — explore outward in layers, nearest nodes first) gives you shortest paths **only when every edge has the same weight**, because it fans out one equal-cost ring at a time. The moment edge weights **differ** (while staying positive), that layered order breaks and BFS fails — **Dijkstra** replaces it: the same idea, but you swap the plain queue for a **min-heap** (a structure that always hands back the smallest-distance node next). If some weights go **negative**, Dijkstra fails too, and **Bellman–Ford** is what handles it. **Tell:** unweighted or uniform-weight → BFS; positive weights → Dijkstra; negative edges → Bellman–Ford.

practice.label: LeetCode 1091. Shortest Path in Binary Matrix

prompt: Explain topological sort: what must be true of the graph, the two standard algorithms, and how you detect that it is impossible.
reveal:
Gist: a **topological sort** lines the vertices up so that **every edge points forward** — if there's an edge u→v, then u comes before v. Picture it as a valid order to do tasks when some tasks depend on others.

It only exists for a **DAG** — a *directed acyclic graph*, one with directed edges and no cycle anywhere. (A cycle would demand some node come before itself, which no ordering can satisfy.)

Two standard algorithms:
- **Kahn's algorithm** repeatedly pulls off any node with **in-degree zero** — no remaining edges pointing *into* it, so nothing is left that must precede it. Keep such nodes in a queue; emit one, delete its outgoing edges (which may drop new nodes to in-degree zero), and repeat.
- **The DFS method** runs depth-first search and pushes each node onto a **stack the moment all of its descendants have finished**; reversing that stack at the end gives the order.

It's **impossible exactly when the graph has a cycle**. Kahn's catches this when it emits **fewer than V nodes** (the ones tangled in a cycle never reach in-degree zero). The DFS method catches it by finding a **back edge** — an edge to a node still sitting on the current recursion stack, meaning you've looped back onto your own path. **Tell:** "ordering with dependencies" plus "no cycles" is the topological-sort signature.

prompt: Why does Dijkstra break with negative edges? Be precise about the invariant that is violated.
reveal:
Gist: **Dijkstra** trusts that the first time it "finalizes" a node, that node's distance is already the best it will ever be. A **negative edge** makes that trust false.

The invariant precisely: Dijkstra always **pops the unvisited node with the smallest tentative distance** and declares it **final**. That's safe only because every *remaining* path to it can add nothing but **non-negative** weight — so no future path could arrive cheaper. (Tentative distance = the best distance found *so far*, not yet confirmed.)

A negative edge violates exactly this: a path that looked longer at pop-time can turn out **cheaper** once it crosses the negative edge later — so a node you already finalized might actually deserve a smaller value. Dijkstra never revisits it, so it silently returns a wrong answer.

**Bellman–Ford** fixes this by never finalizing early: it **relaxes every edge, V−1 times over** (V = number of vertices), which is enough rounds for the true shortest distances to settle. **The tell:** run one *more* pass — pass V — and if any edge still relaxes (still improves a distance), the graph has a **negative cycle**: a loop you can go around endlessly to drive the cost down without bound.

practice.label: LeetCode 787. Cheapest Flights Within K Stops

prompt: Describe union-find with both optimizations and state the resulting complexity. Name two problems where it is the right tool.
reveal:
Gist: **union-find** (also called disjoint-set union) tracks items grouped into sets, answers "are these two in the same set?", and lets you **merge** sets — and with two tweaks it does both in almost constant time. Each set is stored as a tree; every item points toward a **root** that names its set.

**Optimization 1 — union by size (or rank):** when merging two sets, attach the **smaller** tree under the **larger** one's root. This keeps the trees shallow, so walking up to a root stays fast.

**Optimization 2 — path compression:** every time you do a **find** (walk up to the root), re-point each node you passed **directly at the root**, flattening that path for next time.

Together they give **near-constant amortized time** — formally the **inverse Ackermann function α(n)**, which grows so absurdly slowly it stays below 5 for any input you will ever see. ("Amortized" = averaged over a sequence of operations, not guaranteed per single call.)

**Right tool for two jobs:** (1) **Kruskal's MST** — to detect whether adding an edge would **join two separate components** rather than close a cycle; (2) **dynamic connectivity / counting connected components as edges arrive** one at a time. **Tell:** groups merging online plus "same component?" queries.

prompt: Grid BFS with extra state (e.g. fuel, keys, remaining wall-breaks): what goes in the visited set, and what is the pruning invariant?
reveal:
Gist: when a grid search carries **extra state** — fuel left, keys collected, wall-breaks remaining — a cell is no longer simply "visited or not." The same cell reached with **more resources** is a genuinely different, better situation, so your bookkeeping must track the resource, not just the location.

**What goes in the visited set:** the **full state**, `(row, col, extraState)` — not just `(row, col)`. Two arrivals at the same cell with different amounts of fuel are different nodes, and both may be worth exploring.

**The pruning invariant is dominance.** Only revisit a cell if you arrive in a **strictly better** state — more fuel, more keys, more breaks left. An arrival that is **worse or merely equal** on every resource can never lead to an outcome the earlier arrival couldn't already reach, so **prune** it. That one rule is what stops the search from exploding.

**Implementation:** instead of a boolean `visited[r][c]`, keep `best[r][c]` = the **best resource level** seen at that cell so far, and skip any arrival that fails to beat it. **Tell:** a grid BFS/Dijkstra where a move **consumes or grants a budget** — augment the state, prune by dominance.

practice.label: LeetCode 1293. Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination

prompt: Kruskal vs Prim for minimum spanning tree: mechanism, data structure, and which you pick when.
reveal:
Gist: both build a **minimum spanning tree** (MST — the cheapest set of edges that connects every vertex, with no cycles). **Kruskal** thinks in *edges*; **Prim** grows a *tree*.

**Kruskal:** sort **all edges** cheapest-first, then walk down the list adding each edge **unless it would form a cycle** — using **union-find** (the disjoint-set structure) to test in near-constant time whether an edge's two endpoints are already connected. Cost **O(E log E)**, dominated by the sort. Natural on **sparse** graphs and when the input is already an **edge list**.

**Prim:** start from one vertex and **grow a single tree**, each step adding the **cheapest edge that leaves the tree** (connects a tree node to a non-tree node), picked with a **min-heap** (always yields the smallest-weight candidate). Cost **O(E log V)** with a binary heap; the array-based / Fibonacci-heap variant reaches **O(V²)** / **O(E + V log V)**, which is what actually wins on **dense** graphs. It is structurally **almost identical to Dijkstra** — the only change is the heap key: **edge weight** here versus **accumulated distance from the source** in Dijkstra.

**Tell:** sparse or edge-list input → Kruskal; dense or already-have-an-adjacency-structure → Prim.

practice.label: LeetCode 1584. Min Cost to Connect All Points

prompt: Many graph problems give you strings, words, or pairs — not integers. Describe the parse → map → algorithm → unmap pattern.
reveal:
Gist: most graph algorithms are written for **integer-numbered vertices**, but real inputs hand you **strings** — words, course names, airport codes. The fix is a clean four-step pipeline that quarantines the messy relabeling from the clean algorithm.

**Step 1 — parse:** read the input into whatever natural form it arrives in (word pairs, course prerequisites, ticket routes).

**Step 2 — map:** assign each **distinct entity an integer id** using a **hash map** (string → id), and build your **adjacency list** keyed on those ids.

**Step 3 — algorithm:** run the standard **integer-indexed** BFS / DFS / topological sort / Dijkstra completely **untouched** — it never sees a string.

**Step 4 — unmap:** translate the integer answer **back** to the original labels.

**The whole trick is keeping these four steps separate.** Most bugs come from trying to run the algorithm **directly on strings**, tangling the relabeling into the traversal. **Tell:** the input names things with words instead of numbers — build the id map first, and everything after is textbook.

prompt: How do you detect a cycle in a DIRECTED graph with DFS, and why does the undirected method fail here?
reveal:
Gist: to find a cycle in a **directed** graph with DFS, you track not just *whether* a node was visited but *whether it sits on the path you're currently walking*. Three colors do exactly that.

**The three colors:** **white** = unvisited; **gray** = **on the current recursion stack** (you entered it and haven't backed out yet); **black** = fully explored (you finished it and all its descendants). A **cycle exists exactly when DFS reaches a gray node** — you've looped back onto the very path you're still standing on.

**Why the undirected trick fails here:** for undirected graphs you detect a cycle by finding "an already-visited node that isn't my parent." In a *directed* graph, hitting an already-visited **black** node is **perfectly legal** — it just means two paths **converge** on a node you already finished, which is not a cycle. Only a **gray** hit is.

**The point:** the gray-versus-black distinction is what separates **"on my current path"** from **"already done."** Collapse them into one "visited" flag and you get false cycle reports. **Tell:** directed cycle detection = DFS with an on-stack (gray) marker; a back edge to a gray node is the cycle.

prompt: How do you test whether a graph is bipartite, and what does failure tell you about the graph?
reveal:
Gist: a graph is **bipartite** if you can split its vertices into **two groups** so that every edge crosses between the groups (never stays inside one). You test it by trying to **2-color** the graph and watching for a forced conflict.

**The test:** run BFS or DFS; give the start node **color 0**, and give every neighbor the **opposite** color of the current node. If you ever reach an **already-colored** neighbor whose color is the **same** as the current node's, the coloring is impossible — the graph is **not bipartite**.

**What failure means:** a conflict appears exactly when the graph contains an **odd-length cycle**. That is the full characterization — **a graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle** (an even cycle 2-colors cleanly; an odd one always clashes).

**Don't forget:** loop the coloring **over every component**. A disconnected graph can be bipartite in one piece and not in another, so each component must be tested from its own start node. **Tell:** "split into two sides," "two-colorable," or "no odd cycle" all point here.

prompt: What is a strongly connected component, and outline how Kosaraju’s algorithm finds them?
reveal:
Gist: a **strongly connected component (SCC)** is a **maximal clump of vertices that can all reach each other** by following the arrows. **Kosaraju's algorithm** finds every such clump with just two passes of DFS.

**SCC precisely:** a maximal set of vertices where, for any two, there is a **directed path each way** — everyone in the clump can reach everyone else along directed edges. "Maximal" means you can't add another vertex and keep that property.

**Kosaraju, three steps:**
1. Run **DFS on the original graph**, and when a vertex **finishes** (all its descendants are done), **push it onto a stack**.
2. **Reverse every edge** in the graph.
3. **Pop vertices off the stack** in order; from each not-yet-assigned vertex, run **DFS on the reversed graph** — each DFS tree you carve out is **exactly one SCC**.

**Why it works:** the finish-order stack approximates a **topological order of the components** (the highest-finishing vertex lives in a "source" component), and **reversing the edges traps** each DFS inside its own component — it can't leak out into a different one. **The payoff fact:** collapse each SCC to a single node and the result is **always a DAG** (a directed acyclic graph) — the "condensation." **Tell:** mutual reachability in a directed graph, or "condense the graph," signals SCC.

prompt: 0-1 BFS: what problem does it solve, and why can a deque replace a priority queue?
reveal:
Gist: **0-1 BFS** solves shortest paths on a graph where **every edge costs either 0 or 1**, and it reaches **Dijkstra's answer at BFS speed** by swapping the priority queue for a plain **deque** (double-ended queue — you can push and pop at both ends).

**When it applies:** edge weights are only **0 or 1** — extremely common in **grid** problems where some moves are **free** (weight 0) and others **cost one** (weight 1).

**The mechanism:** run a BFS-like loop over a deque. When you relax a **0-weight** edge, push the neighbor onto the **front**; for a **1-weight** edge, push it onto the **back**. This keeps the deque **sorted by distance** at all times, holding **at most two distinct distance values** at once — which is precisely the ordering a **priority queue** (min-heap) would maintain.

**Why it's a win:** you get **Dijkstra's correctness** without Dijkstra's log factor — **O(V+E)** instead of **O(E log V)** (V vertices, E edges) — because the deque keeps order for free instead of paying for heap operations. **Tell:** shortest path where moves are free-or-unit-cost — reach for the deque, not the heap.

practice.label: LeetCode 1368. Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path in a Grid

prompt: What is multi-source BFS and what problem shape signals it?
reveal:
Gist: **multi-source BFS** finds each cell's distance to the **nearest** of many starting points in **one sweep** — you simply seed the queue with **all** the sources at once instead of one.

**The move:** before the BFS begins, **push every source into the queue at distance 0**; then run **one ordinary BFS**. The wavefront expands outward from all sources simultaneously, so each cell is first reached by whichever source is **closest** to it.

**The signal that calls for it:** anything phrased as **"distance to the nearest X"** — nearest exit gate, **rotting oranges** spreading to fresh ones, distance from every cell to the closest 0.

**Why seed them together:** running a **separate BFS per source** costs **O(sources × (V+E))**. Seeding all sources at once gives the **same answer in a single O(V+E) pass** (V cells, E adjacencies), because the merged wavefront already accounts for the closest source to each cell. **Tell:** "nearest among many" distances on a grid → one BFS from all sources.

prompt: Implementing Dijkstra with a binary heap: how do you handle the fact that you cannot decrease-key cheaply?
reveal:
Gist: a binary heap can't cheaply **lower** the priority of an item already inside it (no fast "decrease-key"), so Dijkstra sidesteps the problem: never update — just **push a fresh copy** and ignore the stale ones later. This is **lazy deletion**.

**The trick:** whenever you find a **shorter** distance to a node, **push a new `(distance, node)` pair** onto the heap instead of editing the old one — duplicates are allowed to pile up. When you **pop** a node, first check: is the **popped distance larger than the best distance already recorded** for that node? If so, it's a **stale leftover** from before an improvement — **skip it** and pop again.

**The cost:** the heap can swell to **O(E) entries** (E = edges), giving **O(E log E)**. For simple graphs that is **asymptotically the same as O(E log V)** — because log E and log V differ by at most a constant factor when E ≤ V².

**The alternative and why to skip it:** a *true* decrease-key needs an **indexed heap** (one that tracks each element's position so it can find and sift it). It's fiddly and **rarely worth it in an interview** — lazy deletion is simpler and just as fast asymptotically. **Tell:** "skip if popped distance > best[node]" is the one line that keeps heap-Dijkstra correct.

prompt: When would you use Floyd–Warshall over running Dijkstra from every node? State its structure in one sentence.
reveal:
Gist: **Floyd–Warshall** computes shortest paths between **every pair** of vertices at once, in three tidy nested loops. Reach for it on **small, dense** graphs or when **negative edges** are around.

**When to pick it over running Dijkstra from each node:** (1) you need **all-pairs** shortest paths on a **small, dense** graph — roughly **V ≤ 400–500** vertices; or (2) the graph has **negative edges** (but no negative *cycle*), which plain Dijkstra can't handle.

**Its structure in one sentence:** three nested loops with **k — the intermediate vertex — as the OUTERMOST**, repeatedly applying `dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])` (is it shorter to travel from i to j *via k*?). Cost **O(V³)**.

**Why the loop order matters:** k **must** be outermost so that by the time you consider routing through vertex k, all paths using only intermediates **1..k−1 are already final** — that's the induction that makes it correct. Swap the order and the answers break.

**The trade-off:** on **sparse** graphs, **repeated Dijkstra** wins — **O(V × E log V)** beats O(V³) when E is far smaller than V². **Tell:** "shortest path between all pairs" on a small graph, or negative edges present → Floyd–Warshall.

practice.label: LeetCode 1334. Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors at a Threshold Distance

prompt: How do you combine topological sort with DP? Give the longest-path-in-a-DAG example.
reveal:
Gist: **topological order** processes each node only **after all of its predecessors** — which is exactly the guarantee dynamic programming needs, since DP requires a subproblem's inputs to be solved before the subproblem itself. On a DAG, topo-order + DP is a natural pairing.

**Why they fit:** in topological order, when you reach a node **every edge pointing into it is already finalized**. So the DP has no ordering worries — its dependencies are met by construction.

**Longest path in a DAG, worked:** topologically sort, then relax in that order — `for each node u in topo order: for each edge u→v: dp[v] = max(dp[v], dp[u] + w(u,v))`, where `dp[v]` is the longest path ending at v and `w(u,v)` is the edge weight. The answer is the max over all `dp`. Cost **O(V+E)**.

**Why this is worth internalizing:** **longest path is NP-hard in a general graph** (a cycle lets you loop to inflate the length without limit), yet it's **linear-time on a DAG** — the **acyclicity is exactly what buys you the DP**. **Tell:** the same shape drives **course scheduling, build ordering, and counting paths in a DAG** — spot a DAG plus "longest / best / number of ways," and reach for topo-order DP.

practice.label: LeetCode 329. Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix

prompt: Connected components: when do you use union-find instead of DFS/BFS?
reveal:
Gist: for connected components, **DFS/BFS** is right when the graph is handed to you **all at once**; **union-find** is right when edges **arrive over time** and you must answer "connected?" as they come.

**Use DFS/BFS** when the graph is **static and given up front** — one linear sweep labels every component. It's **simpler and O(V+E)** (V vertices, E edges).

**Use union-find** (disjoint-set union) when either: edges **arrive incrementally** and you must answer **connectivity queries as they stream in**; or the problem is fundamentally about **merging groups** — **Kruskal's MST**, **accounts-merge**, **number-of-islands with streaming additions**. Union-find does each **online merge in near-constant time**.

**Why not just re-run DFS?** Redoing a DFS after **every** new edge would cost **O(E × (V+E))** — quadratic-ish — versus union-find's near-linear total.

**The follow-up trap:** union-find **cannot handle edge deletion** — it only ever merges, never splits. If the problem removes edges over time, neither of these fits cleanly (that needs offline tricks or a more advanced structure). **Tell:** streaming edges plus "same component?" → union-find; one fixed graph → DFS.

prompt: How does A* differ from Dijkstra, and what property must the heuristic satisfy?
reveal:
Gist: **A\*** is Dijkstra with a sense of direction — it prioritizes nodes by **known cost so far plus a guess of the cost still to go**, so the search leans **toward the goal** instead of spreading out evenly in every direction.

**The priority function:** A\* pops the node with the smallest **f(n) = g(n) + h(n)**, where **g(n)** is the actual cost from the start to n (what Dijkstra tracks) and **h(n)** is a **heuristic estimate** of the remaining cost from n to the goal. That forward-looking h is what focuses the search.

**Dijkstra is the special case h = 0** — no guess, so it expands uniformly in all directions.

**The required property:** the heuristic must be **admissible** — it **never overestimates** the true remaining cost. Get that wrong (an overestimate) and A\* can **return a suboptimal path**, because it may commit to a route it wrongly believes is cheap.

**Standard admissible choices on grids:** **Manhattan distance** when movement is **4-directional**, **Euclidean distance** when movement is **free / any-angle** — both never overshoot the real distance. **Tell:** shortest path to a **specific goal** with a cheap distance estimate available → A\* beats plain Dijkstra.

see.label: Red Blob Games — Introduction to the A* Algorithm

prompt: A 2D grid is a graph. State the implicit vertex set, edge set, and the one line of code that generates neighbors.
reveal: A 2D grid is a graph you never have to build. **Vertices** are the cells `(r, c)`; **edges** connect **orthogonally** (or, if allowed, diagonally) **adjacent walkable** cells. Neighbors come from a **direction array**: `for (dr, dc) in [(1,0), (-1,0), (0,1), (0,-1)]`, the neighbor is `(r+dr, c+dc)` — each one guarded by **bounds** (stay on the grid) and **walkability** (not a wall) checks. **Tell:** no explicit adjacency list is needed — the **grid IS the graph**, its edges generated on the fly — and that realization unlocks the entire grid-BFS/DFS family.

prompt: What are the conditions for an Eulerian path and an Eulerian circuit? Contrast with Hamiltonian.
reveal:
Gist: an **Eulerian path uses every EDGE exactly once**; whether one exists is decided by a simple **degree count**. Its cousin, the **Hamiltonian path** (every VERTEX once), has **no** such easy test — and that gap is the whole lesson.

**Eulerian path, undirected:** in a **connected** graph, one exists when **zero or exactly two vertices have odd degree** (degree = number of edges touching a vertex). If **zero** odd-degree vertices, the path closes into an **Eulerian circuit** (starts and ends at the same vertex).

**Eulerian, directed version:** for a **circuit**, **every vertex has in-degree equal to out-degree**; for an open **path**, exactly **one vertex with out − in = 1** (the start) and **one with in − out = 1** (the end), with all others balanced.

**The contrast that matters:** the **Hamiltonian path** — visit every **vertex** exactly once — has **no simple characterization** and is **NP-complete** (no known efficient test exists). So **edges-exactly-once is easy, vertices-exactly-once is hard** — the punchline worth remembering. **Tell:** "traverse every edge / road once" → Eulerian degree check; "visit every city once" → Hamiltonian, suspect NP-hardness.

see.label: cp-algorithms — Finding the Eulerian path in O(M)

prompt: You ran BFS/Dijkstra and have distances. How do you RECONSTRUCT the actual path?
reveal:
Gist: to turn shortest-path **distances** back into the **actual route**, record where you came from as you go — one **predecessor** per node — then walk that chain backward from the target.

**The technique:** keep a **`parent` (predecessor) array**. Whenever the search **relaxes** an edge into v through u — that is, updates v's best distance using u — set **`parent[v] = u`**, remembering that the best way into v came from u.

**Recovering the path:** start at the **target** and follow `parent` **backward** — target, its parent, its parent's parent — until you reach the **source**, then **reverse** the list to read it start-to-finish. Cost is just **O(path length)** and **one extra array**.

**The common mistake:** tracking **only distances** during the search, then trying to **rebuild the path afterward** by re-deriving which neighbors "must have" been on it. That's error-prone and slow — **record the predecessor as you go** and reconstruction is trivial. **Tell:** any time the problem wants the path itself (not just its length), add a parent array before you run the search.

prompt: Why is a minimum spanning tree NOT the same as a shortest-path tree? Give the intuition.
reveal: They optimize **different things**. A **minimum spanning tree (MST)** minimizes the **total weight of the edges** needed to connect **all** vertices — global cheapness of the whole network. A **shortest-path tree** (what Dijkstra builds) minimizes the **distance from one chosen source** to every other vertex. Because the objectives differ, the route between two nodes **inside an MST can be far longer** than their true shortest path. **Tell / intuition:** the MST cares about the **cheapest way to wire everyone together**; Dijkstra cares about **egocentric distance from one root** — same graph, different goal.
